content.content:
Record Rule Draft

A first draft of the record-keeping part of the coordinator skill, and a trial of it on the ten largest entries.

13 Oct 2026 · explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md

The record-keeping part, a first draft

FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only: the language, the library, the tree and your decisions about the project. How the coordinator and you work together goes in the coordinator skill, not in POSITIONS. Both files stay, since workers'

That would move POSITIONS' section on how you want to be spoken to, and the entries of "How we work" that are about you and the coordinator, into the skill. Those two sections come to 49K together, though not all of "How we work" is about y

A FACTS entry states what's true now, and nothing else. Its bold title states the fact.

A sentence stays in an entry only if it changes what a worker or the coordinator does next.

An entry keeps the one number a decision rests on, the test that gates it, as one name or a name pattern, and the report section that holds the rest.

It's a few lines: under about 0.6K for this trial. If it's longer, the pass that wrote it says which decision needs the extra.

Line references, lists of sites, the story of a measurement, timings, counts nobody decides on, and how the fact was found all stay in the report or go to the history.

A POSITIONS entry says what you decided and why, in a breath. Your words appear only where they're the position. What got built is FACTS' to say, the argument stays in the review, and how it was reached goes to the history.

There are three stages. FACTS and POSITIONS are read at every boot and handed out in briefs. The history is opened when a fact's provenance is in question. The report is opened when the detail is needed, and it's the last word.

The coordinator doesn't open the history or a report itself. It sends a worker. A worker takes an entry as given, opens the report section when it needs the detail, and opens the history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

The fortress-repo skill tells a worker what to hand over: each fact in a sentence, the number, the test and the report section. Only the coordinator skill defines the shape of an entry. Workers don't edit FACTS.

The coordinator's pass runs before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. It rewrites what the worker wrote to that shape, moves the worker's text to the history with where it came from, and leaves the detail in the report. In a batch, the com

The pass checks with one search that the report holds what it left out, checks that every key still finds its entry, and reports each entry's size. The old check that nothing's lost still runs, but it isn't the goal.

Sources

1. Your framing, relayed by the coordinator on 13 Oct about 09:20 UTC. Report, Part 2, items 1 to 3.

2. Section sizes: POSITIONS "How we work" 35 entries, 44K, and "How he wants to be spoken to" 6 entries, 4.7K; FACTS "The container" 27 entries, 28K. Report, Part 2, item 4.

content.text:
**Did I run it?** No. The trial checked only three things:
- each entry's size;
- that every citation still finds its entry;
- that the report holds what was cut, with one search each.

Nothing tested whether a reader can still make good decisions from the shorter entries. The cold read and the quiz were planned for after your comments.

**Your test is the right one.** Shrinking only counts if decisions stay as good. This is how I'd run it without you:

1. **Fable writes the scenarios.** It reads the old texts and their reports and writes about eight real decisions. Examples: drafting the next batch's rung, briefing a worker on a checker fix, deciding whether to re-run the distance stage, answering you about the POPL paper as the coordinator, recovering after a process restart. For each one it records the right decision, the facts it needs, and whether those facts belong in the entry or come from following its pointer. Some scenarios are built so the entry alone isn't enough. Those test whether the reader follows the pointer to the source.
2. **Two fresh Opus readers answer them, the way workers would.** Each works in its own copy of the repository:
   - one copy has the old entries;
   - the other has the new entries, with the old texts moved to the history files as a real consolidation would do.

   Both readers can search the record and open reports.
3. **Fable grades the answers blind,** without knowing which copy each came from. It checks two things: is the decision right, and did the reader open the right source when the entry wasn't enough? It also counts how often each reader looked something up.
4. **The pass mark:** the new entries do as well as the old ones on every decision. Wherever they don't, the missing fact goes back into that entry and that scenario runs again. That's how we find the middle ground, entry by entry.

The cost is about 1.2M, an estimate, with about 0.4M of it on Fable. It would run before your comments, so you'd comment with the results in hand.

**The ask:** run it? I recommend yes.

1. `coordinator/README.md:22-26`: "As orchestrator it keeps what a worker or its own next incarnation needs to act: `FACTS.md` (what is established about the language, the library, the runtime and this container, each fact in a few lines with its source and its test, the detail left in the report it cites)".
2. `protocol.md:151-154`, principle 6: "A fact in FACTS with its source and its test, in a few lines with the detail left in the report it cites, and with no date".
3. `coordinator/POSITIONS.md:130`, "The record's form: an optimized build and a debug build.": "A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, pointing to the report or record that holds the detail, a rung's entry too, since rung entries written at full length, about 14 KB a landed batch, are most of FACTS' growth."
4. `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/roles-and-records.md:9`: "`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the language, the library, the run-time and the container, each fact in a few lines with its source and its test, the detail left in the report it cites."

6. `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/records.md:73`: "Its source and its test can be the code at file:line, a gated test, or a command and its output." **Pulls**: it invites a line reference into the entry.
7. `coordinator/FACTS.md:1`: "Established facts: what is true of the tree now, grouped by area, each with its source (a path, a test, a ledger row) and the numbers that describe the tree." **Pulls**: "the numbers that describe the tree" has no limit.
8. `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:791`, the rung's prompt: "The FACTS.md entry the rung earns (the fact, its source and its test in a few lines under a bold title, the detail left in REPORT.md)." Nothing a resumed coordinator needs in order to know the project without Pavol is condensed for length. The test is running. Here's how it's set up:

1. **Fable is writing the scenarios now.** There are eight, covering all ten trial entries:
   - three tasks a worker meets, such as briefing or carrying out a rung;
   - three decisions I make as your assistant: planning the next batch, answering you, a decision about running the work;
   - two built on a fact the new entries cut, where a decision still needs it.

   Each comes with an answer key and a scoring rubric.
2. **Two copies of the repository are ready.** One has the old entries. The other has the new ones, with the old texts in the history files, as a real consolidation would leave them. I've checked that nothing was lost. I removed the trial's report and the boot notes from both copies, so neither reader can tell which copy it has.
3. **Two fresh Opus readers answer next.** Each answers the scenarios in its own copy, and either can open reports and history.
4. **Fable grades the answers.** It won't know which copy each answer came from. Wherever the new entries lead to a worse decision, the missing fact goes back into that entry and the scenario runs again.

It costs about 1.2M, an estimate. You'll get the results before you comment on the page.

usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full stop
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of
                         WORDS: its number, its status and the first 150 characters
                         of its claim (at most 10, then how many more matched)
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as

                         nearest titles are named
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, from the latest of its sections
                         that hold one, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from

  doc:PATH#HEADING       the same for any note, PATH from the repository root, such
                         as a judge's ruling; doc:PATH alone prints the whole note;
                         in a .tex or .tick file the headings are its \chapter, \section,

                         matched with their macros dropped; a heading equal to

                         hold every one of WORDS, a row under its table's header,
                         and the paragraphs whose bold lead holds them
  code:PATH#FROM         the declaration that starts on the one line of PATH that
                         holds FROM, with its line numbers: in .java, .scala and

content.text:
Yes, I follow. FACTS and POSITIONS aren't structured like the ledger, but your tool already treats their titles as keys.

**How it works now**
- **No cells.** Each FACTS or POSITIONS entry is a paragraph, and its bold title is its key. The ledger is the only record with a row template and a tool that writes it.
- **A pointer is a quoted title in the text,** such as `POSITIONS, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`. `facts-extract.sh` takes that quoted title as a query. It finds the entry whose title holds those words, ignoring case and quotes. Its `--check` fails unless exactly one entry matches. So a plain-text reference works as a key by convention, and the tool can resolve it.
- **Where it's used:** the batch script's briefings load entries by these keys. Last night's slices used `--check` to prove that renamed titles still resolve.

**What it doesn't do**
- **Nothing checks every pointer.** The ledger has `ledger.py check`. As far as I know, the pointers inside FACTS and POSITIONS have no equivalent.
- **The tool doesn't follow a pointer.** A brief that quotes a FACTS entry doesn't get the position that entry names. The reader has to run the tool again or search.

With one home and pointers, both gaps matter more. A dead pointer loses a fact, and a brief that quotes one side lacks the other.

**In the test:** the pair worker writes its pointers as quoted titles, and the readers have the skill that names the tool. So the test also shows how a reader follows a pointer: with the tool, by search, or not at all.

**Two small tools would close the gaps,** if the test shows they're needed:
1. A check that every pointer resolves to exactly one entry, run with a consolidation's other checks.
2. An option for `facts-extract.sh` to bring in the entries a quoted entry points to, one level deep.

Both would belong in the record-keeping part.

content.text:
Yes. You're right about where the links matter. FACTS and POSITIONS sit in my context, so I can see their pointers. The history is different: FACTS-history alone is 2.2M characters, with 903 earlier texts in 81 dated sections, and nobody reads it whole.

**How I'd trace an entry today**
- **Its history:** I'd search the history file for the opening words of the entry's title. Each earlier text sits under a dated section, after a comment line that says in prose what became of it. That works while a title keeps its opening words. When an entry is retitled, merged or split, the chain breaks, because the comment line describes the change instead of naming the new title. Last night retitled dozens of entries.
- **Positions on a fact, or facts on a position:** in the current files I search for the quoted title. In the history, old texts carry old titles, so the same search misses them.
- **The tool:** `facts-extract.sh` can fall back to POSITIONS-history for a dated position. It has no query for FACTS-history, and nothing lists which entries point to a given one.

**The ledger already solved this.** Every ledger row has a number that never changes. Its history is filed under "Row N", reports cite the number, and `ledger.py` reads, writes and checks rows by number.

**The same for FACTS and POSITIONS**
- Each entry gets a permanent number, such as F-87 or P-48. The title still says the fact.
- The history files file each earlier text under its number.
- A pointer carries the number, with the title beside it for you.
- The tool resolves a number, prints an entry's history in order, and lists every entry that points to it.
- Renaming a title then costs nothing. Last night's updates of citations across files wouldn't be needed.

**Cost:** numbering the current entries is one script, with no model. Teaching the tool numbers is an Opus worker's job, about 0.3M to 0.5M, an estimate. The 903 old texts can stay filed by date, with numbers only from now on. Mapping them back would be a separate and harder job.

**The ask:** add numbered entries to the record-keeping part's draft, as a proposal for your comments on the page? I recommend yes.

import re, sys
# fill.py <copy dir> <questions.md> <out>: replace each {FACTS n} / {POSITIONS n} line by that copy's entry line n.
root, qpath, out = sys.argv[1:4]
files = {f: open(f'{root}/explorations/coordinator/{f}.md').read().split('\n') for f in ('FACTS', 'POSITIONS')}
def sub(m):
    line = files[m.group(1)][int(m.group(2)) - 1]
    assert line.startswith('- '), (m.group(0), line[:40])
    return line
text = re.sub(r'\{(FACTS|POSITIONS) (\d+)\}', sub, open(qpath).read())
assert '{FACTS' not in text and '{POSITIONS' not in text
open(out, 'w').write(text)
print(out, len(text))

### The ingest 26. The structure of an entry is defined only here. (his words) 27. The `fortress-repo` skill tells a worker what to hand over for FACTS, and not the entry's structure. (his words) What it hands over: each fact as it stands now, in a sentence; the one number a dec 28. The worker writes its full account in its report: the lines, the sites, the figures, and how it found them. (on record: the report holds the detail) It puts the hand-over in a section of its repor 29. The coordinator writes the entry. It rewrites what the worker wrote to this structure, moves the provenance to the history, and leaves the detail in the report. (his words) 30. It does so in a pass before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. (his words: "there should be some post processing. Pass by the coordinator"; that it runs before each batch is on record) In a batch 31. A fact enters FACTS at the pass that follows the commit that establishes it. (new; replaces "in the commit that establishes it") 32. The pass moves the worker's hand-over, verbatim, to `FACTS-history.md`, under the date and with where it came from: the rung, the report, the commit. (new: today the history gets only an earlier t 33. It writes each fact as a new entry, or rewrites in place the entry the fact changes, instead of adding a second. (on record for the rewrite in place) 34. It checks with one bounded `grep` that the cited report section holds each kind of thing it left out. (new) 35. It checks that every key quoting a changed title still resolves, with `facts-extract.sh --check`. (on record as practice) 36. It reports each entry's size, and each entry still over the measure with the decision that needs it. (new) 37. `check-verbatim.py` still runs, since it is cheap. It shows that the history holds the old text. It is not the pass's goal. (on record that it runs; new that it is not the goal) 38. A decision enters POSITIONS in the next commit after he states it, written by the coordinator, and the same pass runs on POSITIONS at each landing and whenever he replaces a decision. (on record)

## 7. What C4 still fails on after decision D

**Answer for the curator.**

With D1, C4 had 14 errors of its own on the compiled checker. That was measured once, on 2026-09-29, on `main` at `6bc21c364` (`reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 2, line 54; the 26 for C4 as written is line 47). None of the 14 comes from the model's own unsized types: D1 clears all 15 of those as such. The 14 split three ways:

- **Arrays, but not the model's types: 4.** Three `DOT`s (`x DOT x`, `y DOT dy`, `p DOT dy` in `rmsn`, `rmsn_b`, `sm_b`) fail because of the library api's dead sizes, sizes that appear in no parameter and no result. That is decision E's E3, and its patch is written and parked (PLAN item 12). The fourth is the `adam` bridge, which passes unsized arrays to `adamN`'s sized parameters. That is a size known only at run time: fork 3.
- **The numerics work: 5.** These are the powers `10.0^(-5)` (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`), `-(10.0^10)` (`:29`) and the check program's three tolerances (`MicroGptFlatCheck.fss:16-18`). Each is refused as "Ambiguous coercion": `RR64`'s `^(self, b:RR64)` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:365`) and `MultiplicativeRing`'s `^(self, other:ZZ64)` (`:283`) both apply only by converting the integer, and neither is more specific (row 533). The refusal comes from the conversion rule built in batch N's rung I, which refuses a tie among converted declarations unless the tie is a numeral's (FACTS, "The compiled checker infers a generic's static arguments with coercion ..."). So yes, five of the 14 come from our numerics work, not from the arrays. They stay under every way of decision D, and the same five are in the 26. They are not a numeral's own type, and that is all the entry's "none is a numeral" means. The same 
  - `numeralTie` (`Functionals.scala:757-797`) reads the numeral as `ZZ32`. `ZZ32` converts into both `RR64` and `ZZ64`, so neither candidate fits without conversion, and neither is more specific.
  - Batch 8 added `^(self, b: IntLiteral)` to the integer types only (`FortressLibrary.fsi:525`, `:577`, `:634`, `:671`). `RR64` did not get one.

  Walk takes all five.
- **Small items: 5.** None of these comes from the arrays or the numerals.
  - `numbersOf` calls `parseRow(line, out, 0)` as a statement and throws its count away (`FlatData.fss:65`), which `blocks.tex:50` refuses.
  - `codePoint`.
  - The varargs `SUM` in `flat`.
  - The varargs export.
  - `matShape`'s body typed `((), ())`. This one is row 474's artefact, not a fault in the model.

  I got this list by matching the 12 of 2026-09-27 (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md` section 5) against the 14 of 2026-09-29: the three `fail` errors went and the five powers came. The entry's "six others" are these five plus the bridge.

**Can you trust 14?** No, not as today's number. It is a floor, and it is stale.

*It is a floor.* Three things hide errors:

- Row 474: an operator applied to a variable of C4's top-level tuple bindings ends its block's check with no error. The diagnostic copy with those bindings split gives 18, not 14, on the same library (array-design-ways line 55).
- A refused statement ends its block. On the split copy with E3, the powers stop `stepN` at its mask line and `adamN` at its update line (line 56). Only the copy with the powers rewritten as well was checked to the end of the step, confirmed by two planted errors. It gave 7 (line 57).
- The entry leaves out a third cause. On 2026-09-27 three bodies crashed on `FortressBuiltin.Character` and were never checked: `parseFloat`, `parseRow` and the check program's `run()` (decision-d-diff section 5). On 2026-09-29 that crash still stood (array-design-ways line 93, row 477). Those bodies contain more powers of row 533's shape, none of them among the five: `10.0^e10`, `10.0^(-e10)` and `10.0^22` (`FlatData.fss:38-40`), and `eps = 10.0^(-6)` (`MicroGptFlatCheck.fss:75`).

*It is stale.* Since 2026-09-29:

- Batch 8 fixed row 477 (`70d5486f9`). Those three bodies are now checked, and `codePoint` may be gone.
- Batch 8's numeral library made the numeral a sibling `IntLiteral` (FACTS, "The one library's numeral type ..."). Row 533 itself says it was "not measured since".

- Batch 13's rung N built fork 3 at 4a, so the checker now opens a size known only at run time (PLAN item 13.3). That may change the bridge.

The re-run passed. With the one sentence about row 533 restored, the new reader scored full marks on that scenario. It found the five numeral powers through row 533, the floor and the date, and offered a fresh measurement as your call. I graded that re-run myself against the same answer key, knowing which copy it came from, so it isn't blind.

**So the test's answer:** with one restored sentence, the shorter entries do as well as the old ones on all ten scenarios. On two they did better, because the long entries buried a fact or carried stale sentences. The one entry that needed more is now 707 characters. That fits the idea that 600 is a check and not a target: an entry can go over it when a decision needs the extra.

**The cost was over my estimate.** The test wrote 2.49M against the 1.6M I gave you. The grader alone wrote 0.75M, and Fable wrote 1.26M in all.

**Corrected in the record on the way:** the `MatchFailure` sentence in FACTS, and the row 516 sentence in your instance-rule position.

**Next:** a worker is adding the test to the draft report and to the page as a section called "The test". It's also saving the scenarios and answer key as a kit, so the trial boot can reuse them. I'll give you the page when it's done. Your comments on the page come after that.
